lessons.title: What HTML is

cards.title: The skeleton of a page
cards.compare: A house has a frame: walls, rooms, doors. Paint and furniture come later.
cards.simple: [[HTML]] is the skeleton of a web page. It says: this is a title, this is a paragraph, this is a picture.
cards.normal: [[HTML]] gives a web page its **structure**. It tells the browser what each part is: a heading, a paragraph, a list, an image, a link.
cards.technical: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) describes document structure and meaning. The browser parses it into a tree called the DOM, which [[CSS]] styles and [[JavaScript]] can change.

cards.title: HTML is labels, not math
cards.compare: Like putting sticky labels on parts of a document: "Title", "Important", "Note".
cards.simple: HTML doesn't calculate anything. It only **labels** things. That's why it's called [[markup]].
cards.normal: HTML is a [[markup]] language, not a programming language. It can't add numbers or make decisions — it only describes content. That makes it the easiest place to start.
cards.technical: Being declarative, HTML has no variables, conditions or loops. Logic comes from [[JavaScript]] (in the browser) or [[PHP]] (on the server, generating HTML).

cards.title: The three partners
cards.compare: Skeleton (HTML) + clothes (CSS) + muscles that move (JavaScript).
cards.simple: **HTML** = what it is. **CSS** = how it looks. **JavaScript** = what it does.
cards.normal: Every web page uses up to three languages: [[HTML]] for structure, [[CSS]] for style, and [[JavaScript]] for behavior. Today we focus on the skeleton.
cards.technical: Separation of concerns: keep content in HTML, presentation in CSS, behavior in JS. This makes pages easier to maintain, more accessible and faster.

cards.title: HTML is just a text file
cards.compare: Like a letter written in Notepad — nothing magic.
cards.simple: An HTML file is plain text. Its name ends with `.html`. You can write one in Notepad.
cards.normal: An HTML file is plain text saved with `.html` at the end. Open it in a browser and the browser turns the labels into a real page. A [[code-editor|code editor]] like VS Code makes it easier.
cards.technical: HTML files are UTF-8 text served with the `text/html` content type. The server can send a static `.html` file or generate HTML dynamically (as WordPress does with PHP).
cards.code:
Hello, NRCP!

This is my first web page.

recap: [[HTML]] is the structure (skeleton) of every web page.
It labels content; it doesn't calculate.
HTML = what it is, CSS = how it looks, JS = what it does.
lessons.atMyJob: In the WordPress editor, click the ⋮ menu → **Code editor**. Everything you see there is HTML that WordPress saves for your post. Your theme's PHP files also output HTML.

quiz.q: What is HTML's job?
Is HTML a programming language?
options: No, it's a markup language that labels content
quiz.explain: Right! It describes — it doesn't calculate.

lessons.title: Tags: the labels of HTML

cards.title: What a tag looks like
cards.compare: Like putting a word between two bookends.
cards.simple:
A [[tag]] is a word inside pointy brackets, like `

`. It means "a paragraph starts here."
cards.normal:
A [[tag]] is a label inside angle brackets `< >`. `

` opens a paragraph. `

` (with a slash) closes it.
cards.technical:
Tags delimit elements. An opening tag `

`, content, and a closing tag `

` with a forward slash. Tag names are case-insensitive but written lowercase by convention.

cards.title: Open and close
cards.compare: Opening and closing a bracket in math: ( … ).
cards.simple: Most tags come in pairs. One opens. One closes. The closing one has a slash: `/`.
cards.normal: Tags usually come in pairs. Together with the content, they form an [[element]]. Forgetting to close one is a very common [[bug]].
cards.technical: An [[element]] = opening tag + content + closing tag. Browsers try to fix missing closing tags, but results may be unexpected — always close them.

cards.title: Some tags are alone
cards.compare: Like a stamp — one mark, nothing inside.
cards.simple:
Some tags have nothing inside, so they don't need closing. Example: `` for a picture, `
` for a new line.
cards.normal:
Some elements are **empty** (void) — they have no content, so there's no closing tag. Examples: `` (image), `
` (line break), `
` (line), ``.
cards.technical:
Void elements: area, base, br, col, embed, hr, img, input, link, meta, source, track, wbr. You may see `
` — the slash is optional in HTML5.

cards.title: Attributes: extra details
cards.compare: Like writing "FRAGILE" or "Deliver to Room 3" on a box label.
cards.simple: Tags can have extra details inside. These are [[attribute|attributes]]. Example: `src` tells which picture to show.
cards.normal: [[Attribute|Attributes]] add information to an opening tag. They're written `name="value"`. Example: ``.
cards.technical: Attributes live in the opening tag only. Common global attributes: id, class, style, lang, title, hidden. Values should be quoted. Boolean attributes (like `disabled`) need no value.

cards.title: Boxes inside boxes
cards.compare: A small box inside a bigger box. Close the small one first.
cards.simple: You can put tags inside tags. That's [[nesting]]. Close the inside one first.
cards.normal: Elements can sit inside other elements — that's [[nesting]]. Rule: **last opened, first closed**.
cards.technical:
Nesting builds the DOM tree (parent/child). Mis-nesting like `

hi

` is invalid; browsers repair it in unpredictable ways.

recap:
A [[tag]] is a label in angle brackets: `

` closes.
Some tags (like ``) are alone and don't close.
[[Attribute|Attributes]] add details; tags can be nested inside each other.
lessons.atMyJob: When a WordPress post layout looks broken (everything turned bold, or a sidebar dropped down), a missing closing tag is often the reason. Switch to Code editor and look for an unclosed `<strong>` or `<div>`.

lessons.title: The basic page structure

cards.title: Every page has the same frame
cards.compare: Every official letter has the same parts: letterhead, body, signature.
cards.simple: Every HTML page starts the same way. Learn this frame once, use it forever.
cards.normal: All HTML pages share a basic frame: a [[doctype]] line, then `<html>`, which holds a [[head]] and a [[body]].
cards.technical: Minimal valid HTML5: doctype, html (with lang), head (meta charset, viewport, title) and body.

cards.title: The DOCTYPE line
cards.compare: Like the form number at the top: "This is Form 2026-A."
cards.simple: The first line, `<!DOCTYPE html>`, tells the browser: "This is a modern web page."
cards.normal: [[DOCTYPE]] tells the browser to use modern HTML rules. Without it, the browser may act in an old, strange way.
cards.technical: `<!DOCTYPE html>` triggers standards mode. Omitting it causes quirks mode, emulating old browser bugs (different box model, etc.).

cards.title: The head: info about the page
cards.compare: The back office of a store: paperwork, not displays.
cards.simple: The [[head]] holds info **about** the page, like its title in the browser tab. You don't see it on the page.
cards.normal: The [[head]] contains information about the page: the `<title>` (shown on the tab), `<meta>` settings, and links to [[CSS]] files. It's not shown as page content.
cards.technical: Head contents: title, meta (charset, viewport, description), link (stylesheets, icons, manifest), script, base. Search engines and social sites read these.

cards.title: The body: what you see
cards.compare: The store's display floor where customers walk.
cards.simple: The [[body]] holds everything you see: words, pictures, buttons.
cards.normal: The [[body]] contains all visible content. Everything from the logo to the footer goes inside `<body>`.
cards.technical: Body content is usually organized with [[semantic]] sections: `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<article>`, `<aside>`, `<footer>`.

recap: Every page: [[DOCTYPE]] → `<html>` → `<head>` + `<body>`.
[[head]] = info about the page (title, settings).
[[body]] = everything you see.
lessons.atMyJob: In a WordPress theme, `header.php` prints the DOCTYPE, `<head>` and the start of `<body>`. `footer.php` closes the body and html. Plugins add things into the head using a function called `wp_head()`.

quiz.q: Where does the page title (shown on the browser tab) go?
Where do pictures and paragraphs go?
quiz.explain: Correct — the body is everything you see.

lessons.title: Headings and paragraphs

cards.title: Headings: h1 to h6
cards.compare: Like a newspaper: big headline, smaller sub-headlines.
cards.simple: Headings are titles. `<h1>` is the biggest. `<h6>` is the smallest.
cards.normal: There are six heading levels: `<h1>` (main title) down to `<h6>`. Use them in order, like an outline — not just to make text big.
cards.technical: Headings define the document outline. Screen reader users jump between headings; search engines use them for context. Use one `<h1>` per page and don't skip levels.

cards.title: Paragraphs
cards.compare: Like paragraphs in a letter — each one a block of related sentences.
cards.simple:
Normal text goes in `

`. Each `

` is one paragraph.
cards.normal:
`

` holds a paragraph of text. Pressing Enter in your HTML file does **not** make a new line on the page — you need a new `

` (or `
`).
cards.technical:
Browsers collapse whitespace: multiple spaces and line breaks become one space. Use `

` for paragraphs, `
` only for line breaks within content like addresses.

cards.title: Important and emphasized words
cards.compare: Like underlining words with a marker when you read.
cards.simple: `<strong>` makes words important (usually **bold**). `<em>` adds emphasis (usually *italic*).
cards.normal: `<strong>` = important, shown bold. `<em>` = emphasis, shown italic. These carry **meaning**, so screen readers can stress them.
cards.technical: Prefer [[semantic]] `<strong>`/`<em>` over presentational `<b>`/`<i>`. Visual styling belongs in CSS.
cards.code: Please back up before updating. It is really important.

recap: Headings `<h1>`–`<h6>` work like an outline.

`

` makes paragraphs; Enter in your file doesn't.
`<strong>` = important, `<em>` = emphasis.
lessons.atMyJob: In WordPress, the post title is usually the `<h1>`. Inside your post, use **Heading 2** and **Heading 3** blocks for sections — never another H1. This helps Google and screen-reader users, which matters for government accessibility standards.

quiz.q: Which heading is the biggest / most important?
quiz.explain: Yes — h1 is the main heading.

lessons.title: Links and images

cards.title: Links: doors between pages
cards.compare: A door from one room to another.
cards.simple: A link takes you to another page. It uses the `<a>` tag and an `href` that says where to go.
cards.normal: A [[hyperlink]] uses `<a href="…">`. The `href` [[attribute]] is the destination [[URL]]. The text between the tags is what people click.
cards.technical: Anchor element `<a>`. href can be absolute (`https://…`), relative (`about.html`), a fragment (`#contact`), `mailto:` or `tel:`. Add `target="_blank" rel="noopener"` to open safely in a new tab.

cards.title: Good link text
cards.compare: A door sign that says "Kitchen" is better than one that says "Door".
cards.simple: Write link text that says where it goes. Not "click here".
cards.normal: Good link text describes the destination: "Download the 2026 annual report" instead of "click here". It helps everyone, especially screen-reader users.
cards.technical: Screen readers can list all links out of context, so "click here" ×10 is useless. Descriptive link text also helps SEO.

cards.title: Images
cards.compare: Hanging a framed photo on the wall.
cards.simple: `` shows a picture. `src` says which picture.
cards.normal: `` shows an image. `src` is the file location. It's a single tag — no closing.
cards.technical: Use `width`/`height` to prevent layout shift, `loading="lazy"` for below-the-fold images, and modern formats (WebP/AVIF). `srcset` lets the browser pick sizes.

cards.title: Alt text: describe the picture
cards.compare: Like describing a photo to a friend over the phone.
cards.simple: [[alt text|Alt text]] describes the picture in words. Blind users hear it. It also shows if the picture fails to load.
cards.normal: The `alt` attribute is a text description for screen readers and broken images. Describe what matters: "Graph showing funding rose in 2026". Purely decorative images get `alt=""`.
cards.technical: alt is required for valid HTML and [[accessibility]] compliance (WCAG 1.1.1). Empty alt marks decorative images so screen readers skip them.

recap: Links: `text` — use clear link text.
Images: ``.
[[alt text|Alt text]] helps blind users and shows when images fail.
lessons.atMyJob: When you upload to the WordPress Media Library, fill in **Alternative Text** — that becomes the `alt` attribute. For links in posts, use the link button and write meaningful text like "Apply for the research grant".

quiz.q: Which attribute tells a link where to go?
why: src is for images (the picture's source).

quiz.q: Which is the best link text?
quiz.explain: Exactly — it says where it goes.

lessons.title: Lists

cards.title: Bullet lists
cards.compare: A grocery list — order doesn't matter.
cards.simple: `<ul>` makes a bullet list. Each item goes in `<li>`.
cards.normal: `<ul>` = unordered list (bullets). Each item is an `<li>` (list item). Use it when order doesn't matter.
cards.technical: `<ul>` contains only `<li>` children. Navigation menus are usually a `<ul>` inside `<nav>`, styled with CSS.

cards.title: Numbered lists
cards.compare: Cooking steps — order matters!
cards.simple: `<ol>` makes a numbered list. Use it for steps.
cards.normal: `<ol>` = ordered list (numbers). Use it for steps where order matters, like instructions.
cards.technical: `<ol>` supports `start`, `reversed` and `type` attributes. Screen readers announce "list, 3 items" for both types.
cards.code:
1. Back up the site
  2. Update plugins
  3. Test the site

cards.title: Lists inside lists
cards.compare: Main topics with sub-points, like an outline.
cards.simple: You can put a list inside a list item. Great for menus with sub-menus.
cards.normal: Nest a new `<ul>` or `<ol>` **inside** an `<li>` to make sub-items. WordPress dropdown menus are built this way.
cards.technical: The nested list must be a child of `<li>`, not of `<ul>` directly. WordPress `wp_nav_menu()` outputs nested `<ul class="sub-menu">`.

recap: `<ul>` = bullets; `<ol>` = numbers.
Every item is an `<li>`.
Nested lists go inside an `<li>` (like sub-menus).
lessons.atMyJob: Your WordPress navigation menu is really a `<ul>` list of links. Right-click the menu on your site in a desktop browser → **Inspect** to see the `<ul>` and `<li>` tags.

quiz.q: Which list is best for step-by-step instructions?
quiz.explain: Yes — ordered lists show numbered steps.

lessons.title: Forms: letting visitors send information

cards.title: A paper form, but online
cards.compare: An application form with blanks to fill in and a Submit button.
cards.simple: A [[form]] lets visitors type and send things, like a message or a search.
cards.normal: A [[form]] collects information. It's made of `<form>` containing inputs (boxes to type in) and a submit button.
cards.technical: `<form action="/submit" method="post">` sends named fields to the server. GET puts data in the URL (searches); POST puts it in the request body (logins, messages).
cards.code:
<form action="/send" method="post">
  <label for="name">Your name</label>
  <input id="name" name="name">
  <button>Send</button>
</form>

cards.title: Inputs and labels
cards.compare: Each blank on a paper form has a printed label next to it.
cards.simple: `<input>` is a box to type in. `<label>` is its name tag. Always use both.
cards.normal: Every `<input>` needs a `<label>`. Connect them: the label's `for` matches the input's `id`. Then tapping the label focuses the box, and screen readers read it aloud.
cards.technical: Input types: text, email, tel, number, date, password, checkbox, radio, file. The right type shows the right iPhone keyboard (e.g. `type="email"` shows @).

cards.title: Where does the data go?
cards.compare: You drop the paper form in a box; someone in the office reads it.
cards.simple: When you press Send, the form goes to the [[server]]. Code there (like [[PHP]]) reads it.
cards.normal: HTML only **shows** the form. Something on the [[server]] — like PHP or a WordPress form [[plugin]] — must receive and process the data.
cards.technical: The server reads POST fields (PHP: `$_POST['name']`). Always validate and sanitize on the server — browser checks (`required`) can be bypassed. Protect against spam with CAPTCHA or honeypots.

recap: A [[form]] = `<form>` + inputs + a button.
Every input needs a `<label>`.
The server (PHP / a plugin) processes the data — HTML only shows the form.
lessons.atMyJob: Contact or feedback forms on your agency site usually come from a plugin (like Contact Form 7 or WPForms). The plugin writes the HTML form and the PHP that emails or stores the message. If forms stop sending, check the plugin and the server's email settings.

why: label is the name tag next to the box.

quiz.q: Who actually processes the form data after you press Send?

quiz.explain: Right — HTML only shows the form.
